passage: "People ask me what it's like sharing a hostel room with Farhan. Honestly? Normal. I'm Sumit. Farhan has tics: his arm jerks, and he says 'yup' a lot, loudly, not because he means yes. First week, I noticed. I didn't say anything. What would I say? We were arguing about whose turn it was to buy milk, and I just kept arguing. When other guys asked 'What's his deal?', I said, 'He's my roommate. He's fine.' About a month in, Farhan brought it up himself, late at night. 'You never asked about the tics.' I said, 'Didn't seem my business. Anything I can do?' He thought, then said, 'Just what you're doing.' Then he beat me at cards."

qa.q: What did Sumit and Farhan argue about in the first week?
qa.a: Whose turn it was to buy milk.

qa.q: What does Farhan saying 'You never asked about the tics' suggest he felt?
qa.a: It suggests he noticed and appreciated that Sumit treated him normally, and felt accepted.

qa.q: Which of Sumit's choices made Farhan feel accepted?
qa.a: Sumit never commented or asked Farhan to stop, carried on normally, and only talked about the tics when Farhan raised them.

qa.q: How might Sumit feel when Farhan says 'Just what you're doing'?
qa.a: Sumit may feel reassured and glad that simply treating Farhan normally was the right thing to do.

grounding: It shows a wise roommate who does not comment on or imitate tics, carries on normally and acknowledges them only when the person raises it.

passage: I'm Ira, and I've worked with Aparna for two years. I learned something from her in a team meeting last week. A new analyst, Kunal, joined us. During his first presentation his shoulder jerked, and he made a quick sniffing sound, again and again. A couple of people glanced at each other. One raised an eyebrow at me. Aparna didn't glance at anyone. She kept her eyes on Kunal's slides and asked, "Can you go back to the chart on sales by region?" as if nothing else was happening. The others followed her lead. Afterwards, by the coffee machine, Kunal said to her, "I have tics, by the way." She said, "Thanks for telling me. Anything you'd like from us?" He said, "No, that was perfect."

qa.q: What did Aparna ask Kunal to go back to?
qa.a: The chart on sales by region.

qa.q: What does Kunal's reply 'that was perfect' suggest about how he felt?
qa.a: It suggests he felt accepted and relieved that the team treated him normally.

qa.q: Which of Aparna's choices set the tone for the team?
qa.a: She kept her eyes on the slides and carried on the discussion, not glancing at anyone, and the others followed.

qa.q: How might the colleague who raised an eyebrow see things after watching Aparna?
qa.a: They might realise that carrying on normally is the respectful response, not exchanging looks.

grounding: A colleague watches a wise coworker who ignores tics respectfully, carries on the conversation and acknowledges them only when the person raises it.

passage:
Monday: On Rehana's first day at the library internship, her head jerked sideways and she made a sharp squeak mid-sentence. A visitor at the counter laughed. Imran, cataloguing beside her, just said, "So the old maps go on shelf C?" and carried on.
Wednesday: At lunch, Rehana's tics came fast, three squeaks in a row. Imran didn't look up from his rice. "Did you finish the map labels? They look great."
Friday: As they locked up, Rehana said, "You've never asked about my tics." Imran shrugged. "Figured you'd tell me if you wanted." She smiled. "I do. They're tics, and they get worse when I'm new somewhere." "Thanks for telling me," he said, and they walked to the bus stop talking about Monday's exhibition.

qa.q: Where do Imran and Rehana work?
qa.a: They work at a library internship.

qa.q: How did Rehana feel when she brought up her tics on Friday?
qa.a: She felt accepted and comfortable enough to explain, smiling because Imran had never made an issue of them.

qa.q: Why was Imran's way of responding wise?
qa.a: He never commented, stared or asked her to stop, kept the conversation going and only talked about the tics when she raised them.

qa.q: How does Imran seem to see Rehana's tics?
qa.a: Imran seems to see them as simply part of Rehana, nothing that needs comment, questions or fixing.

grounding: Shows a friend who does not comment, imitate or ask for tics to stop, carries on the conversation and acknowledges them only when the person raises it.

passage: "Chetan, you're nervous about the new intern with tics? Let your Sarika Didi tell you what she did wrong at your age. When I was twenty-two, a colleague named Victor used to make a sharp barking sound and twitch his arm. In our first meeting I said, 'Can you please stop that? The client can hear.' He went red and didn't speak for the rest of the day. I felt terrible. After that, I learned: I just carried on talking. I didn't look away, I didn't copy, I didn't ask. Weeks later he said, 'Sarika, thanks for never making it a thing.' Then he told me about it himself, over tea. He became my closest friend in that office. So with your intern: talk about the work. Let them bring it up."

qa.q: What sound did Victor make?
qa.a: He made a sharp barking sound and twitched his arm.

qa.q: How did Sarika feel after asking Victor to stop?
qa.a: Sarika felt terrible and guilty when he went red and stayed silent all day.

qa.q: What choice inside the story built trust between Sarika and Victor?
qa.a: She stopped commenting or asking, carried on normally and let Victor raise his tics when he chose, which later led to friendship.

qa.q: How might Victor have felt when Sarika asked him to stop in front of others?
qa.a: He likely felt humiliated and hurt, which is why he went red and did not speak for the rest of the day.

grounding: An elder recalls learning to respectfully ignore a colleague's tics, carrying on the conversation and acknowledging them only when he raised it.

passage: The café was packed, the project was due at nine the next morning, and Pradeep and Deepika had four slides left. Deepika's vocal tic, a short "hup," came every few seconds, louder when she was stressed. A man at the next table turned and glared. Pradeep didn't look at him or at Deepika's mouth. He kept pointing at the laptop. "This graph needs a title. What about 'Water use by ward'?" Deepika nodded. "Hup. Yes. Good." They finished at eleven. Walking out, she said, "That guy was staring." Pradeep said, "I noticed. Does it bother you when people do that?" "Sometimes. Thanks for just carrying on." "Always," he said.

qa.q: What title did Pradeep suggest for the graph?
qa.a: He suggested 'Water use by ward.'

qa.q: How did Deepika feel about Pradeep carrying on with the work?
qa.a: She felt grateful and accepted, thanking him for just carrying on despite the man's stare.

qa.q: What did Pradeep do that made Deepika feel accepted?
qa.a: He ignored the tic, kept working on the slides and only talked about it when Deepika raised the staring, asking how it felt for her.

qa.q: How might Pradeep feel when Deepika thanks him?
qa.a: He likely feels glad and a little moved, answering "Always" to show he will keep treating her the same way.

grounding: Shows a friend who does not comment on or stop a person's tics, keeps working with her and acknowledges them only when she raises it, despite a noisy café and a deadline.

passage:
Hafsa and Nitin were planning the college fest budget sheet over cutting chai at the canteen in Lucknow. Every few sentences, Nitin's throat made a sharp "hup" sound and his shoulder twitched.
A boy at the next table stared and nudged his friend. Hafsa didn't look up. "So if the stall rent is split four ways," she said, "we can afford the sound system."
Nitin went "hup" again. Hafsa kept writing.
When the sheet was done, Nitin paused. "You never ask about my tics."
"You never brought them up," Hafsa said. "I figured you'd tell me if you wanted to."
"Most people either stare or tell me to stop." He smiled. "Thanks for just planning a fest with me."
"You're the best at spreadsheets. Obviously I'm planning with you."

qa.q: Where were Hafsa and Nitin planning the fest?
qa.a: At the canteen, over cutting chai.

qa.q: Why did Hafsa keep writing when Nitin made the sound?
qa.a: She felt calm and respectful, wanting Nitin to feel normal rather than watched, so she carried on the conversation.

qa.q: What did Hafsa's approach get right?
qa.a: She didn't comment, imitate or ask him to stop, and only acknowledged the tics when Nitin raised them, which made him feel accepted.

qa.q: How does Nitin see Hafsa by the end?
qa.a: He admires and appreciates her for treating him as a friend and the best at spreadsheets, not a curiosity.

grounding: Hafsa does not comment on or react to Nitin's tics and carries on the conversation, acknowledging them only when he raises them, which makes him feel accepted.
